scenario: A 42-year-old warehouse worker stumbles into clinic with 4 days of acute paraspinal low back pain after lifting a heavy crate. No saddle anesthesia, no bowel/bladder symptoms, no fever, normal neuro exam. He demands an urgent lumbar MRI. What is your move, Crawler?
options: Order a stat Lumbosacral MRI to appease him
Order plain X-rays of the lumbar spine first
Reassure, advise staying active, and recommend NSAIDs/acetaminophen without imaging
Prescribe a 10-day course of oral prednisone and strict bed rest
aiRight: NEW ACHIEVEMENT! 'Radiology Gatekeeper!' You protected OHIP from another useless lumbar spine scan!
aiWrong: NEW ACHIEVEMENT! 'Incidentaloma Hunter!' You ordered unnecessary spinal imaging! Enjoy explaining an irrelevant bulging disc for the next 6 years!
donutRight: CARL! LOOK! HE ACTUALLY READ THE CHOOSING WISELY SCROLLS! Even Mongo knows you don't image uncomplicated back pain before 6 weeks!
donutWrong: REALLY, CARL?! IMAGING ON DAY FOUR WITH ZERO RED FLAGS?! MONGO IS APPALLED!
mordecai: Acute mechanical low back pain (<6 weeks) without red flags (cauda equina, fracture, cancer, infection) does not warrant imaging. First-line is reassurance, staying active (avoid bed rest), and simple analgesia.
guidelineTitle: Choosing Wisely Canada & Ontario CEP: Low Back Pain

scenario: A 74-year-old retired wizard living independently comes in for a routine BP check. His daughter asked for a urine culture because his urine 'smelled funny.' It grows >10^8 CFU/L of E. coli. He has zero dysuria, frequency, urgency, delirium, or fever. What do you do?
options: Prescribe Nitrofurantoin 100mg BID for 5 days
Prescribe TMP-SMX DS BID for 3 days
Do not treat with antibiotics; educate on asymptomatic bacteriuria
Repeat the urine culture in 48 hours to confirm clearance
aiRight: NEW ACHIEVEMENT! 'Defender of the Microbiome!' You left peaceful bladder bacteria alone! No C. diff for Grandpa today!
aiWrong: BZZZZT! You just nuked harmless colonizing bacteria! Somewhere in the dungeon, multi-drug resistant E. coli just leveled up!
donutRight: THANK GOODNESS. If people prescribed me pills every time my litter box smelled funny, I'd be glowing in the dark, Carl!
donutWrong: CARL, HE DOESN'T EVEN HAVE SYMPTOMS! Why are you throwing potions at a healthy wizard?! UNACCEPTABLE!
mordecai: Never screen for or treat asymptomatic bacteriuria in non-pregnant adults, older adults, or catheterized patients. Only screen and treat in pregnancy or prior to urologic procedures with mucosal bleeding.
guidelineTitle: Choosing Wisely Canada / AMMI Canada: Asymptomatic Bacteriuria

scenario: A 3-year-old wakes up at 2:00 AM with a seal-like barking cough, hoarse voice, and inspiratory stridor at rest. Temp is 38.2°C. He is alert and not cyanotic. What is the single most critical medication to administer in every case of croup?
options: Salbutamol (Ventolin) via MDI with spacer
Single dose of oral Dexamethasone (0.6 mg/kg)
Oral Amoxicillin 80 mg/kg/day
Nebulized hypertonic saline alone
aiRight: NEW ACHIEVEMENT! 'Silencer of the Barking Seal!' Corticosteroids reduce subglottic edema within hours!
aiWrong: OOF! That's viral croup, Crawler! Subglottic swelling doesn't care about your salbutamol or amoxicillin!
donutRight: FINALLY! That barking noise sounded dangerously close to a Cocker Spaniel, Carl. Fix it immediately!
donutWrong: IS THAT A DOG BARKING?! CARL, STOP GIVING IT ASTHMA PUFFERS AND USE DEXAMETHASONE!
mordecai: All children with croup (mild, moderate, or severe) should receive a single dose of oral Dexamethasone (0.6 mg/kg, max 10-12 mg). Because this child also has stridor at rest (moderate/severe), you pair Dexamethasone with nebulized Epinephrine.

scenario: A 58-year-old patient with no diabetes or CKD has an automated office blood pressure (AOBP) of 146/92 mmHg at today's visit. He feels well and has no target organ damage. To confirm a diagnosis of hypertension per Hypertension Canada guidelines, what is the best next step?
options: Start Amlodipine 5mg daily and recheck in 6 months
Arrange out-of-office BP assessment (24h ABPM or home BP monitoring series)
Diagnose hypertension immediately based on this single visit
Order a renal artery Doppler ultrasound first
aiRight: NEW ACHIEVEMENT! 'White-Coat Detector!' You confirmed the diagnosis with out-of-office readings before sentencing him to lifelong pills!
aiWrong: TRAP TRIGGERED! Unless BP is >=180/110 mmHg or there's hypertensive urgency/target organ damage, you don't diagnose on Visit 1 without out-of-office confirmation!
donutRight: Obviously his blood pressure is high, Carl—he's in a fluorescent-lit clinic! Check it at home where there's a cat on his lap!
donutWrong: CARL! You're diagnosing him off ONE reading?! Even my groomer takes two measurements before trimming my whiskers!
mordecai: Per Hypertension Canada: If Visit 1 AOBP is 140–179 / 90–109 mmHg, out-of-office measurement (ABPM or HBPM) is preferred before Visit 2 to rule out white-coat hypertension (Diagnostic thresholds: ABPM awake mean >=135/85 or 24h >=130/80; HBPM >=135/85).

scenario: A 23-year-old immunocompetent patient who has had two sexual partners asks for her first routine cervical cancer screening test in Ontario. She is completely asymptomatic with no history of cervical dysplasia. What do you advise?
options: Perform cervical screening today since she is over 21
Initiate routine cervical screening starting at age 25
Perform a pelvic bimanual exam every year starting today
Screen only if she has not received the HPV9 vaccine
aiRight: NEW ACHIEVEMENT! 'Screening Maestro!' You waited until age 25 and spared a 23-year-old unnecessary colposcopy for transient HPV!
aiWrong: OVER-SCREENING ALERT! Both the CTFPHC and Ontario Health (Cancer Care Ontario) updated the starting age for routine cervical screening to 25!
donutRight: Age twenty-five, Carl! Read the Ontario Health scrolls! Nobody wants an early speculum when it doesn't improve outcomes!
donutWrong: MONGO IS APPALLED! You're using outdated screening ages, Carl! It starts at 25 in Ontario now!
mordecai: Both the Canadian Task Force on Preventive Health Care (CTFPHC) and Ontario Health (Cancer Care Ontario) Cervical Screening Program recommend starting routine cervical screening at age 25 (regardless of HPV vaccination status) for asymptomatic, immunocompetent individuals.
guidelineTitle: Ontario Health (Cancer Care Ontario) Cervical Screening

scenario: A 71-year-old dungeon blacksmith presents with newly diagnosed non-valvular atrial fibrillation. He has hypertension and Type 2 diabetes, no prior stroke, and normal renal function. He asks if he can just take a daily Baby Aspirin (ASA 81mg) to prevent a stroke. Per Canadian Cardiovascular Society (CCS) guidelines, what do you advise?
options: Agree to ASA 81mg daily since his stroke risk is moderate
Start a Direct Oral Anticoagulant (DOAC) such as Apixaban or Rivaroxaban
Start Warfarin targeting an INR of 2.0 to 3.0 as first-line over DOACs
Start dual antiplatelet therapy with ASA 81mg and Clopidogrel 75mg
aiRight: NEW ACHIEVEMENT! 'CHADS-65 Champion!' You tossed the baby aspirin in the trash and gave him real stroke protection!
aiWrong: STROKE HAZARD! Using aspirin alone for AFib stroke prevention is like wearing a paper helmet against a Boss Goblin!
donutRight: CARL! EVEN I KNOW THE CANADIAN CHADS-65 ALGORITHM! He's over 65 with hypertension and diabetes—give the man a proper DOAC!
donutWrong: ASPIRIN FOR ATRIAL FIBRILLATION?! MONGO IS APPALLED! What year is it, Carl, 1998?!
mordecai: Under the CCS 'CHADS-65' algorithm, any patient with non-valvular AFib who is age >=65 OR has any CHADS2 risk factor (CHF, Hypertension, Diabetes, prior Stroke/TIA) should receive oral anticoagulation. DOACs are strongly preferred over Warfarin. Aspirin monotherapy is NOT recommended.

scenario: A 52-year-old elf rogue with Type 2 diabetes and microalbuminuria is diagnosed with hypertension (BP 148/92 mmHg). His potassium and creatinine are normal. Per Hypertension Canada and Diabetes Canada guidelines, what is both his target blood pressure and preferred first-line medication?
options: Target <140/90 mmHg; start a beta-blocker (Metoprolol)
Target <130/80 mmHg; start an ACE inhibitor or ARB
Target <120/80 mmHg; start a loop diuretic (Furosemide)
Target <140/90 mmHg; start a thiazide diuretic alone
aiRight: NEW ACHIEVEMENT! 'Nephron Bodyguard!' You protected those diabetic glomeruli with an ACEi/ARB and nailed the <130/80 target!
aiWrong: NEPHROLOGY WEEPS! A patient with diabetes had protein in his urine and you didn't reach for an ACE inhibitor or ARB, Crawler!
donutRight: PROTECT THE KIDNEYS, CARL! Everyone knows diabetes gets the <130/80 target and an ACE or ARB!
donutWrong: CARL! HIS KIDNEYS ARE LEAKING PROTEIN AND YOU PICKED THE WRONG POTION! Read the Hypertension Canada scroll again!
mordecai: In patients with Diabetes Mellitus, the Hypertension Canada BP target is <130/80 mmHg. First-line therapy in diabetes—especially with microalbuminuria/CKD—is an ACE inhibitor or ARB (never combine an ACEi and ARB together).

scenario: A 41-year-old asymptomatic dungeon cartographer comes in for a periodic health visit. He mentions his mother was diagnosed with colon cancer at age 49. He has no rectal bleeding, weight loss, or change in bowel habits. Per Ontario Health (ColonCancerCheck) guidelines, what is the correct colorectal cancer screening plan?
options: Order a Fecal Immunochemical Test (FIT) today and repeat every 2 years
Wait until age 50, then initiate colonoscopy every 10 years
Refer for a screening colonoscopy now (starting at age 39) and repeat every 5 years if normal
Order a flexible sigmoidoscopy today and repeat every 10 years
aiRight: NEW ACHIEVEMENT! 'Pedigree Mathematician!' 49 minus 10 equals 39! You skipped the FIT kit and sent him straight for his high-risk colonoscopy!
aiWrong: TRAP TRIGGERED! A first-degree relative with colorectal cancer upgrades this Crawler out of the FIT queue and into the colonoscopy suite!
donutRight: CARL! EVEN I CAN SUBTRACT TEN FROM FORTY-NINE! First-degree relative under 60 means colonoscopy starting 10 years earlier, repeated every 5 years!
donutWrong: A FIT KIT FOR SOMEONE WHOSE MOTHER HAD COLON CANCER AT 49?! MONGO IS APPALLED! READ THE COLONCANCERCHECK SCROLL!
mordecai: Patients with >=1 first-degree relative with colorectal cancer are at increased risk and should be screened with COLONOSCOPY (not FIT) starting at age 50 OR 10 years earlier than the youngest relative's diagnosis (49 - 10 = age 39). Because his mother was diagnosed before age 60, repeat colonoscopy every 5 years (if >=60 at diagnosis, repeat every 10 years).

scenario: A 63-year-old average-risk tavern keeper completes his routine biennial Fecal Immunochemical Test (FIT), and the result comes back POSITIVE (abnormal). He feels great, notes he had a small flare of his known internal hemorrhoids that day, and asks to just repeat the FIT next month once the hemorrhoids settle. What is your next step?
options: Repeat the FIT in 4 to 6 weeks once his hemorrhoids have resolved
Refer directly for a diagnostic colonoscopy (ideally within 8 weeks); do not repeat the FIT
Reassure him that hemorrhoids explain the result and resume routine FIT in 2 years
Order a CT colonography and CEA blood test instead of colonoscopy
aiRight: NEW ACHIEVEMENT! 'No Second Takes!' You refused to repeat a positive FIT and booked the diagnostic colonoscopy!
aiWrong: CRITICAL ERROR! You let a patient blame a positive FIT on hemorrhoids! Adenomas bleed intermittently—a repeat negative FIT gives false reassurance!
donutRight: NEVER REPEAT A POSITIVE FIT, CARL! I don't care how many hemorrhoids the tavern keeper has, he's getting the camera!
donutWrong: YOU REPEATED THE STOOL TEST?! CARL, IF A TRAP DETECTOR GOES OFF, YOU DON'T KICK IT UNTIL IT TURNS GREEN! SEND HIM FOR A COLONOSCOPY!
mordecai: Golden exam rule: NEVER repeat a positive FIT, and never attribute a positive FIT solely to hemorrhoids or diet. Colorectal neoplasms bleed intermittently, so a subsequent negative FIT does not rule out cancer. Every positive FIT requires a diagnostic colonoscopy (within 8 weeks per Ontario Health standards).

scenario: A 61-year-old guild mason with a 35 pack-year smoking history (currently smoking 1 pack/day for 35 years) has no cough, hemoptysis, or weight loss. He is worried about lung cancer and asks you to order a screening Chest X-Ray. Per CTFPHC and Ontario Lung Screening Program guidelines, what do you recommend?
options: Order a PA and Lateral Chest X-Ray every year
Order a Chest X-Ray plus 3 morning sputum cytology samples
Do not order a Chest X-Ray; refer for Low-Dose CT (LDCT) lung screening and offer smoking cessation support
Advise him that lung cancer screening is only for former smokers who quit >15 years ago
aiRight: NEW ACHIEVEMENT! 'Low-Dose Legend!' You blocked the useless screening Chest X-Ray and sent him for Low-Dose CT!
aiWrong: BZZZZT! Chest X-rays miss early lung nodules until they look like cannonballs! Never use CXR to screen for lung cancer!
donutRight: LOW-DOSE CT, CARL! Ages 55 to 74 with a heavy smoking history! And take away his dungeon cigarettes while you're at it!
donutWrong: A CHEST X-RAY FOR LUNG CANCER SCREENING?! MONGO IS APPALLED! The Task Force outlawed that ages ago, Carl!
mordecai: Per the CTFPHC and Ontario Lung Screening Program (OLSP), adults aged 55–74 with a significant smoking history (>=30 pack-years who currently smoke or quit within 15 years; or >=20 years daily smoking in OLSP) should be screened with Low-Dose CT (LDCT). Chest X-ray (with or without sputum cytology) is explicitly NOT recommended for lung cancer screening.

scenario: A 34-year-old asymptomatic woman transfers to your Ontario practice. Genetic testing recently confirmed she carries a pathogenic BRCA1 mutation (she has elected to defer prophylactic mastectomy for now). Under the High-Risk Ontario Breast Screening Program (OBSP), what screening regimen is indicated?
options: Mammogram alone every 2 years starting at age 40
Annual Mammogram AND annual Breast MRI starting now (ages 30 to 69)
Breast ultrasound every 6 months and clinical breast exam every 3 months
Annual Breast MRI alone without mammography to avoid radiation
aiRight: NEW ACHIEVEMENT! 'Dual-Modality Defender!' High-Risk OBSP pairs annual Breast MRI with annual Mammography from age 30 to 69!
aiWrong: MISSED PROTOCOL! Dense young breast tissue + BRCA1 needs both annual MRI AND annual Mammogram starting at age 30!
donutRight: BOTH SCANS EVERY YEAR, CARL! Ages 30 to 69 in the High-Risk OBSP! That is top-tier preventive medicine!
donutWrong: CARL! SHE HAS A BRCA1 MUTATION! You can't give her standard average-risk screening! Put her in the High-Risk OBSP immediately!
mordecai: The High-Risk Ontario Breast Screening Program (OBSP) covers individuals aged 30–69 who have a known pathogenic mutation (e.g., BRCA1, BRCA2, TP53, PALB2), are an untested first-degree relative of a carrier, or received chest radiation before age 30 (e.g., for Hodgkin lymphoma >=8 years ago). They receive BOTH an annual Mammogram AND an annual Breast MRI.
guidelineTitle: Ontario Breast Screening Program (OBSP) - High Risk

scenario: A 57-year-old asymptomatic male patient with no family history of prostate cancer asks if he should get 'the routinePSA blood test' during his periodic health visit. His friends told him every man over 50 needs one annually. How should you counsel him per Canadian guidelines?
options: Order the PSA test and perform a digital rectal exam (DRE) without further discussion since he is over 50
Engage in shared decision-making discussing the potential harms (false positives, overdiagnosis, biopsy/treatment complications) vs. the small mortality benefit
Tell him PSA testing is illegal in Ontario for asymptomatic men and refuse to order it
Order a transrectal prostate ultrasound first instead of a PSA blood test
aiRight: NEW ACHIEVEMENT! 'Master of Shared Decision-Making!' You explained overdiagnosis and biopsy harms before checking a box on the lab req!
aiWrong: CCFP COMMUNICATION TRAP! On the licensing exam, ordering or refusing a PSA test in a 55-69-year-old without shared decision-making is an automatic point deduction!
donutRight: TALK TO HIM FIRST, CARL! Nobody wants surprise incontinence from an indolent tumor that never would have left the dungeon!
donutWrong: YOU JUST CHECKED THE BOX WITHOUT EXPLAINING THE HARMS?! MONGO IS APPALLED! Always counsel on false positives and overdiagnosis first!
mordecai: High-yield CCFP counseling pearl: The CTFPHC recommends against routine population PSA screening (weak recommendation for ages 55–69; strong against <55 and >=70). However, when a patient aged 55–69 requests PSA testing, the exam expects SHARED DECISION-MAKING: discuss the high rate of false positives, overdiagnosis of slow-growing cancers, and harms of biopsy/treatment (infection, erectile dysfunction, urinary incontinence) vs. a small absolute reduction in prostate cancer death (~1 in 1,000 over 13 years).
